In addition, trip requests can be served by multiple AV fleets, operated by various entities, either public or private, and complemented by a rich mix of other manual modes including micromobility. The hard realities of overcoming the technical challenges of designing and deploying a fully automated AV-based transport system have been highlighted in the last several years, as many startup AV companies have ceased operations or turned their development to other aspects of robotics. Even very large companies with substantial financial resources to devote to research and development of AV technology have been withdrawing from the prospective new market or scaling back their investments over the last few years because of the considerable challenges. However, some companies have “stayed the course” and are progressing from early deployment and demonstrations to initial scaling of services. The business case for AMD implementation depends on the balance of capital and operating costs with the revenue streams generated by the services as well as agreements with public authorities in which AMDs may operate. Various private (nonautomated) transportation services such as taxis, limousine services, and commercial ride-hailing services such as Uber and Lyft (referred to herein as transportation network companies [TNCs]) operate for profit, whereas the revenue side of public transit services typically relies on subsidies in addition to fare charges. Public costs also exist for private transportation services, such as the access to public right-of- way and street infrastructure, which may not be as overt as for public modes. Other modes of transportation are integrated into the value of a commercial development and are offered for free. For example, parking is often subsidized by other aspects of a development, such as having parking costs validated by a retail entity, and internal movement within a facility such as elevators, escalators, and moving walkways is amortized into the cost of building development. In these situations, the value in the investment of a transportation system is realized, or returned, apart from ridership fares. Now that mature automated driving systems (ADS) are becoming a reality, additional challenges must be met for a successful business case for deploying AV technology on a large scale within an AMD. One additional challenge is addressing accessibility across various population subgroups. The cost of AV technology deployment combined with the associated provisions for Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) compliance can conflict with the need to offer transport fare at sufficiently low prices that all economic levels of the population can use the services yet high enough to maintain adequate return on investment. Part of the answer in achieving comparable access to all groups may be in providing subsidized fares for some who are economically disadvantaged and unsubsidized, full-fare pricing for those who can readily afford this service—as is applied to nutrition in the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program. Another approach may be that the transport service within a district is freely available to all—in much the same way that elevators, escalators, or moving walkways function in large buildings and facilities—with related costs absorbed in the operational budget of the facility.
